## Process for rerandomization simulation

To generate simulation data I did the following for each outcome $j$ in our set of outcomes across our empirical dataset (excepting a few studies that were inaccessible):

1) Load the empirical data for outcome $j$, patch missing data, etc.
2) Calculate the empirical estimates of the treatment effects for outcome $j$, and the associated empirical standard errors.
3) Repeatedly, for simulation runs $r = 1, \ldots, R$, permute the treatment assignment across clusters and within blocks.  I then re-estimated the impacts given the permuted assignment.
4) I then, within each run and outcome, calculated the range of estimates, and the ratio of the largest to smallest standard error, across all the estimators that were defined for that run. I did this both overall, and for the group of estimators within each estimand (Person or Cluster).
5) I finally saved the set of results to a file. 

Due to the permutation, there is no actual treatment effect.
Any actual treatment effect is pushed into individual and cluster variation.
For example, if a cluster had a positive average effect, the permutation simulation views this cluster as just having a slightly higher intercept than it would have had, had it been a control cluster in reality.
The structure of the data, the relationship of covariates to outcome, etc., is all preserved by this approach.


## The datasets missing from this analysis

We didn't run the simulation on all the empirical datasets due to privacy restrictions and computational feasibility.  The datasets dropped are the following:

```{r}
miss_sets %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, n, J ) %>%
  knitr::kable( caption = "Dropped Datasets" ) %>%
  print()
```




# How do the simulation estimated SEs compare to the actual simulation SE?

Within the simulation, we can compare the average estimated SE to the standard deviation of point estimates across the permutations.  We include the actual empirical data as one of the "simulation permutations."

```{r}

ggplot( meth_dat, aes( SE, ESEhat ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ method ) +
  geom_point() +
  coord_fixed() +
  geom_abline( slope=1, intercept=0, lty=2 )

```

Some methods do not have standard errors, so they are not in the above plot.
Counts of the methods with and without standard errors are below.

```{r}
meth_dat %>%
  group_by( method ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             SE_def = sum( !is.na( SE ) ),
             ESEhat_def = sum( !is.na( ESEhat ) ) ) %>%
  arrange( desc( ESEhat_def ), method ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```


# The actual vs. permutation estimates

For each study, we can look at the actual ATE range from the empirical data (red dot) vs. the ranges we get from the permutations (the boxplot).

```{r}
if ( FALSE ) {
  range_dat %>%
    filter( Estimand == "Overall" ) %>%
    group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
    summarise( sdRange = sd( rangeATE ),
               sdRatio = sd( ratioSE ) ) %>%
    knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
}

range_dat_o = range_dat %>%
  filter( Estimand == "Overall" ) 

emp_dat <- range_dat_o %>%
  filter( runID == "empirical" )

# Plot the ranges of ATE estimates (over all estimators)
ggplot( range_dat_o, aes( UniqueID, rangeATE ) ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point( data=emp_dat, color="red" ) +
  coord_flip()
```

Weirdly, for the curated data, all the actual ranges are quite low.  We also see notable differences between the two sets of data, with curated having much wider ranges in general.


We can look at the range of ATE estimates vs size of study (number of clusters):

```{r}
rr <- range_dat_o %>%
  left_join( studies, by="UniqueID" )
rr_emp = filter( rr, runID == "empirical" )

ggplot( rr, aes( n, rangeATE, color=Collection, group=UniqueID ) ) +
  geom_boxplot( outliers = FALSE ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection ) +
 # geom_point( data=rr_emp, color="red" ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs( x = "Number of clusters",
        y = "Range of ATE estimates",
        title = "Range of ATE estimates by number of clusters" )
```

For reference, here are the set of empirical results:

```{r}
ggplot( rr_emp, aes( J, rangeATE, color=Collection, group=UniqueID ) ) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection ) +
 # geom_point( data=rr_emp, color="red" ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs( x = "Number of clusters",
        y = "Range of ATE estimates",
        title = "Range of ATE estimates by number of clusters" )

```


### Variation in Standard Errors

We next look at how much the ratio of the max to min estimated standard errors vary across the permutations

```{r}
range_dat %>%
  filter( Estimand == "Overall" ) %>%
  ggplot( aes( UniqueID, ratioSE ) ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point( data=emp_dat, color="red" ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "Variation in Ratio of maxSE to minSE" )
```

We again look by number of clusters (the dots are the empirical values):

```{r}
ggplot( rr, aes( J, ratioSE, color=Collection, group=UniqueID ) ) +
  geom_boxplot( outliers = FALSE ) +
  geom_point( data=rr_emp, col="red", size=0.5 ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Collection ) +
 # geom_point( data=rr_emp, color="red" ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs( x = "Number of clusters",
        y = "Range of ATE estimates",
        title = "Ratio of SE estimates by number of clusters" )

```



# Imposter Plots

We then insert the real estimated values as an "imposter" so we could see if the estimated distributions looked like the actual one.
